Let’s talk about Chapter 8: The Ongoing Struggle—Change, Backlash, and the Work Ahead.
You know, when real change starts happening, it almost never goes off without a hitch. For every bit of progress, there’s usually some kind of pushback—a reminder that old habits just don’t let go that easily, and those holding onto power rarely give it up without a fight.
The journey we’ve seen in “Men Explain Things to Me” isn’t a straight shot to success. It’s more like winding through a maze, with moments of hope mixed in with setbacks and resistance.
Imagine this: your workplace rolls out a new policy meant to make meetings more inclusive, so everyone gets a chance to speak. At first, there’s real excitement—people feel like something good could happen. But then, almost on cue, the grumbling starts. Some folks complain it’s overkill, that men are being singled out, or that the issue’s being blown out of proportion. Suddenly, the conversation shifts away from women’s voices being ignored, and now it’s about whether the new rules are fair or even necessary.
Sound familiar? It’s a pattern we see again and again. Whenever a marginalized group starts making progress, there’s a tendency for those in power to feel threatened. The backlash can look like jokes at someone’s expense, dismissive eye rolls, or just quietly slipping back into old routines. Sometimes it’s even more obvious—like when policies get rolled back or voices are outright silenced.
What most people don’t realize is how exhausting it is to keep pushing against that kind of resistance. There’s always this temptation to just give in, to settle for small wins and call it a day. But here’s something important: the stories in this book remind us that, even when the going is slow, change is possible. Every act of resistance, every moment when people stand together, matters. Over time, these small efforts add up—and the culture begins to shift, often in ways you don’t notice until you look back and realize just how much has changed.
One thing becomes clear: the work is never truly finished. There will always be new hurdles, fresh ways for voices to be dismissed, and challenges that demand a response. But there’s hope, too—a sense that with each new generation, more people are included in the conversation, and the circle of those who are truly heard gets a little bit wider.
This struggle isn’t confined to big public debates or policies. It happens in the quiet moments, too—in chats with friends, at family gatherings, in the everyday choices people make. The work goes on, but so does the potential for real change.
